articles.title: Relator do ajuste fiscal na Câmara mantém texto do Senado; projeto deve ser votado na segunda-feira | G1
articles.standfirst: Deputado Mauro Benevides já disse que evitaria mudanças para aprovação do texto ser acelerada; ajuste economiza R$ 50 bilhões em 2027.
articles.summary: Deputado Mauro Benevides já disse que evitaria mudanças para aprovação do texto ser acelerada; ajuste economiza R$ 50 bilhões em 2027.
articles.body:
O relator do projeto de ajuste fiscal do governo Lula (PT) na Câmara dos Deputados , Mauro Benevides (União Brasil-CE), apresentou nesta quinta-feira (19) seu parecer para a proposta . Benevides manteve o mesmo texto aprovado pelo Senado.

O texto deve ser votado na noite de segunda-feira (23) na Câmara dos Deputados. Normalmente, os deputados não costumam fazer votações às segundas, mas o presidente da Câmara, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), decidiu acelerar a votação .

Deputado Mauro Benevides (União-CE), relator da proposta na Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: Kayo Magalhães/Câmara dos Deputados

A ausência de mudanças no parecer de Benevides tem o mesmo motivo. O deputado afirma que uma aprovação rápida do ajuste fiscal de Lula deve mandar uma boa sinalização sobre a economia brasileira para o mercado e para a sociedade.

O objetivo do governo é conter o crescimento das despesas públicas e aumentar a arrecadação para tentar estabilizar a dívida pública, preservando políticas sociais.

Depois da passagem pelo Senado, o projeto encabeçado pelo ministro do Planejamento, Bruno Moretti, manteve suas principais medidas. Entre elas, estão:

um limite de 2% para o crescimento de gastos em anos nos quais contingenciamento seja necessário; e

a efetivação de uma defesa antiga do governo: um novo corte linear de 10% em benefícios que o governo dá aos mais diferentes setores da economia.

O ministro do Planejamento e Orçamento, Bruno Moretti. — Foto: Fábio Rodrigues Pozzebom/Agência Brasil

Apesar da dificuldade de votação no Senado, com críticas do setor produtivo e da oposição, o caminho na Câmara promete ser mais rápido. Benevides já começou o trabalho de conversar com as bancadas dos partidos para angariar apoio e a ideia é aprovar o ajuste fiscal o mais rápido possível.

🔎 Atualmente, empresas que possuem créditos tributários podem deixar de pagar outros impostos, mesmo que sejam de origem diferente dos que deram direito ao crédito.

Pelo projeto, o governo poderá estabelecer restrições a essas compensações, com percentuais diferenciados conforme o valor. A medida poderá ser adotada em momentos nos quais o governo entre em contenção de gastos.

Em manifestações separadas, divulgadas em 12 de novembro, CNI, Fiesp e a Federação das Indústrias do Estado de Minas Gerais (Fiemg) sustentaram que os grandes empresários arcarão com a maior parte do custo do ajuste.

Na prática, a restrição pode aumentar a arrecadação em dinheiro no curto prazo, porque parte dos tributos que seria pago com créditos terá de ser efetivamente paga, com dinheiro, pelas empresas.

articles.title: Moraes libera ações sobre Lei da Dosimetria para julgamento no STF; caso será analisado em dezembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Julgamento será realizado no plenário virtual, entre 4 e 15 de dezembro. Com aplicação suspensa desde maio, lei permitiria a redução de penas de condenados pelos atos de 8 de janeiro de 2023.
articles.summary: O STF julga em dezembro ações que questionam a Lei da Dosimetria, que pode reduzir a pena de 27 anos de Jair Bolsonaro e de outros condenados pelos ataques de 8 de janeiro de 2023.
articles.body:
O ministro Alexandre de Moraes , do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), liberou nesta quinta-feira (19) para julgamento ações que questionam a chamada Lei da Dosimetria, que prevê a redução de penas para condenados por atentados golpistas no país.

O caso será analisado no plenário virtual do Supremo, entre os dias 4 e 15 de dezembro.

Ministros do STF afirmam de forma reservada que haveria maioria na Corte para manter a dosimetria, com eventuais propostas de ajustes.

🔎 A lei permite a redução de penas de condenados pelos ataques de 8 de janeiro de 2023, incluindo a pena do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), condenado a 27 anos e três meses de prisão no julgamento da trama golpista, e aliados dele. A lei foi vetada integralmente pelo presidente Lula (PT), mas o Congresso Nacional derrubou posteriormente o veto (relembre abaixo) .

A aplicação da lei está suspensa desde maio deste ano (veja mais abaixo).

um mecanismo para tornar mais rápida a progressão do regime de pena (quando um condenado sai de uma modalidade mais severa e passa para um regime mais brando) para quem cumpre pena por crimes contra o Estado Democrático de Direito;

redução de até 2/3 da pena imposta aos vândalos comuns dos ataques de 8 de janeiro de 2023;

que o crime de tentativa de golpe de Estado (com penas maiores) vai absorver o de tentativa de abolição do Estado, em caso de condenação simultânea.

Dados do Supremo indicam que 455 condenados podem ser beneficiados pela lei da dosimetria . Eles foram condenados por tentativa de abolição do Estado Democrático de Direito e golpe de Estado.

A lei impede que as penas desses dois crimes sejam somadas quando ocorrerem no mesmo contexto. Com isso, passa a valer a pena do crime mais grave (Golpe de Estado, de 4 a 12 anos) com um acréscimo de 1/6 até a metade.

Nesta semana, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), e o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), se reuniram com Moraes e pediram que o ministro liberasse as ações para julgamento do plenário do STF sob o argumento de que foi uma lei aprovada há quase um ano pelo Congresso Nacional .

Em maio, o ministro suspendeu a aplicação da lei. Com isso, os condenados pelos atos golpistas de 8 de janeiro de 2023 passaram a depender de uma decisão do plenário para obter o benefício da redução de suas penas.

Moraes aplicou o entendimento a casos de condenados que já haviam acionado a Corte com o pedido de revisão da pena com base na legislação recém-aprovada.

Condenado a 27 anos e três meses de prisão no julgamento da trama golpista, Bolsonaro não chegou a pedir a redução da pena, embora a lei tenha sido articulada por seus aliados e motivada, em parte, pela condenação do ex-presidente.

A defesa do ex-presidente pediu duas vezes a revisão criminal da trama golpista. O procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet, já defendeu que o STF rejeite os pedidos . Com o parecer, o ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, relator do caso, já pode levar o caso a julgamento.

A revisão criminal é uma ação que permite contestar uma condenação que já se tornou definitiva, em situações previstas em lei, como diante do surgimento de novas provas.

Ministros ouvidos pelo g1 afirmam que a dosimetria é um caminho alternativo à revisão criminal apresentada pela defesa de Bolsonaro.

Isso porque ela, na prática, diminuiria o tempo de cumprimento da pena de Bolsonaro, aliados e condenados pelos ataques de 8 de janeiro, sem necessariamente criar um novo embate na Corte.

Alexandre de Moraes em sessão plenária do STF — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

Aprovação da dosimetria, veto de Lula e retomada do PL

Aprovada em dezembro de 2025, a Lei da Dosimetria permite a redução de penas de condenados pelos ataques de 8 de janeiro de 2023 , incluindo a pena do ex-presidente Bolsonaro e de aliados.

Em janeiro de 2026, o presidente Lula vetou integralmente o projeto de lei. Em abril, o Congresso Nacional derrubou o veto do presidente, retomando os efeitos do PL da dosimetria.

Na Câmara, foram 318 votos favoráveis à derrubada do veto e 144 contrários. No Senado, foram 49 votos para a derrubada do veto e 24 votos contra.

Antes da votação, Alcolumbre adotou uma manobra para evitar conflito com outra lei em vigor. Ele retirou da análise do Congresso um trecho do PL da Dosimetria por contrariar a chamada Lei Antifacção, que havia endurecido regras para progressão de regime.

O trecho retirado pelo presidente do Senado, na prática, facilitava a progressão de regime para condenados por crimes graves, como feminicídio e crimes hediondos.

articles.title: STF: Ministros recebem relatório da PF sobre Daniel Vorcaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao menos cinco ministros confirmaram que o material foi disponibilizado pela presidência do STF. Segundo os relatos, os documentos não trazem informações sobre colegas, apenas citações a eles.
articles.summary: Documentos da PF sobre o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro foram entregues aos ministros do STF citados e à PGR, gerando preocupação com possíveis desgastes na Corte.
articles.body:
O presidente do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), Edson Fachin, enviou uma cópia dos relatórios produzidos pela Polícia Federal (PF) sobre as relações do banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, aos ministros que foram citados no material.

Ao menos cinco ministros confirmaram que o material foi disponibilizado pela presidência do STF. Segundo esses relatos, os documentos só trazem citações a eles. Não há informações sobre colegas.

Ao todo, a PF entregou 10 relatórios a Fachin. Desses, seis já foram arquivados. O presidente do STF encaminhou à Procuradoria-Geral da República (PGR) quatro "para exame e avaliação das providências que entender cabíveis" em 15 dias.

Caberá à PGR avaliar se o conteúdo justifica a abertura de uma apuração, se é preciso aprofundar os fatos narrados com novas diligências, se há dados para medidas mais gravosas, como uma denúncia, ou se é o caso de arquivamento.

Além disso, Fachin informou que as informações recebidas serão mantidas, no momento, em sigilo.

O diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Rodrigues, se reuniu na noite de quarta-feira (18) com Fachin para entregar o relatório citando todos os ministros do tribunal mencionados ou que trocaram mensagens com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

Também participaram da reunião o diretor-executivo da PF, William Murad, e o diretor de Combate ao Crime Organizado e à Corrupção, Dennis Cali.

O material deve detalhar menções e citações aos ministros sem avançar sobre condutas criminosas ou não. Os documentos chegam ao STF quando a primeira fase da Operação Compliance Zero, que investiga as fraudes do Master e suas conexões, completa um ano.

Após encontro, Andrei afirmou que entregou todos os relatórios demandados pela Corte e um HD com todas as mensagens citando ministros da Corte no caso Master.

Segundo ele, os relatórios dos delegados foram considerados inadequados não pelo conteúdo em si, mas pela forma como foram produzidos.

Ministros em sessão no plenário do STF — Foto: Gustavo Moreno/STF

A confirmação da reunião entre o diretor-geral da PF e o presidente do STF provocou um clima de tensão no STF.

Nos bastidores, há preocupação entre os ministros com as providências que serão adotadas pelo presidente da Corte após receber o material.

O receio é de que, a depender das medidas tomadas pelo presidente, o Supremo enfrente novos desgastes, embates públicos e vazamentos sobre as condutas de ministros.

articles.title: Trump’s CISA pick Michael LoSapio rejects Jan. 6 as an 'attack,' won't name 2020 election winner
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's pick to lead an agency with a key role in protecting U. elections told senators during a confirmation hearing Thursday that he would...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's pick to lead an agency with a key role in protecting U.S. elections told senators during a confirmation hearing Thursday that he wouldn't characterize the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection as an "attack."

The response by Michael LoSapio, nominated to head the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, came as part of an exchange with U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who has made inquiries about the violence and the 2020 election part of his line of questioning for a number of Trump nominees.

It's also part of Republicans' rush to confirm Trump's picks before Democrats take power in Congress early next year.

"No, I don't believe it was an attack," LoSapio told Blumenthal. "I wasn't involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news."

The White House did not immediately return a request seeking comment on the remark by LoSapio, who if confirmed would inherit an agency mired in partisan tensions over the role it should play in combating false claims about voting or election fraud.

He also isn't the first Trump nominee to answer the Jan. 6 question similarly.

During his own June confirmation hearing for the post of Department of Justice inspector general, Don R. Berthiaume — also during questioning from Blumenthal — acknowledged "violence on the Capitol grounds" on Jan. 6, 2021, but also said, "I don't know if I would use the term attack."

Several of Trump's judicial nominees have also shied away from characterizing the violence as an "attack" during their own confirmation hearings.

On Thursday, Blumenthal also asked LoSapio, currently chief information security officer at artificial intelligence firm Palantir, who won the popular vote in the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed that he won.

"I'm not going to answer the question about an election six years ago," LoSapio said, later adding that his "only involvement" in that election was voting for Trump.

CISA — formed in 2018 during the first Trump administration and nested within the Department of Homeland Security — is charged with protecting the nation's critical infrastructure, from dams and nuclear power plants to banks and voting systems.

It's received bipartisan praise from many state and local election officials, but Trump and his allies remain angry over its efforts to counter misinformation about the 2020 presidential election and the coronavirus pandemic.

The agency's first director, Chris Krebs, was fired by Trump after highlighting election officials' statement calling the 2020 election the " most secure in American history."

CISA has also been without a Senate-confirmed director for nearly two years. Jen Easterly left the agency as Trump returned to office last year, and Nick Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Sean Plankey withdrew in April when his nomination stalled.

images.caption: Michael LoSapio, nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, appears before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs for confirmation, at the Capitol in Washington, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite)

articles.title: $1M-a-day China tech crackdown proposed amid cascade of US cyber disruptions
articles.summary: Rep. Pat Harrigan says his Digital Infrastructure Act of 2026 would bar high-risk carriers from U.S. data centers and cloud services, with $1M daily fines.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., wants to close a glaring national-security loophole that allows Chinese entities to cohabitate the same data centers where critical American services also run. The North Carolina lawmaker is proposing the Digital Infrastructure Act of 2026 to address the potential risk with a $1 million-per-day fine for violators. Meanwhile, the U.S. has experienced a series of outages and incidents this week that have put a microscope on the potential for foreign cyber threats and have prompted skepticism regarding U.S. readiness to defend against digital weaknesses. "Look, the federal government already determined that companies like China Telecom and China Unicom posed a threat to our national security and revoked their licenses to operate here," Harrigan said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "But those companies were still able to maintain connections inside of American data centers. So, if we think about that, we determined that they were too dangerous to operate here, but we left them with a foothold in the very infrastructure that carries Americans' information." CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Despite the cascade of outages — including in U.S. air traffic control systems, Microsoft and banking services —Harrigan did not directly draw a line between Chinese companies and the disrupted services. There is also no proof that any of the incidents were the result of cyberattacks. Harrigan, instead, argued that preventing cyber vulnerabilities in the future requires lawmakers to eliminate what they know to be weaknesses now. "What we're talking about is the infrastructure that supports our banks, our hospitals, our businesses and our communication systems," Harrigan said. He declined to elaborate on whether the existing loophole has already led to cyberattacks or stolen data but noted that he was made aware of the liability when American businesses approached him with concerns. His bill would prohibit high-risk carriers from owning or operating a data center in the U.S. or offering cloud services to Americans. The measure would be enforced by a $1 million fine for every day of a continuing violation — a penalty that would extend to affiliates and even American venture partners doing business with Chinese entities. The bill also includes a time-limited exception for companies approved by American communications officials. CHINA’S GREAT AI CHIP LOOPHOLE: HOW AMERICAN ESPIONAGE STOPPED CHINA — THIS TIME "We talked to a lot of companies, frontier labs and data center owners, as well as operators that are concerned about this," Harrigan said. "And it's also part of folks from our national security apparatus within government." As part of its mission, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) reviews foreign communication companies and green-lights their operation in the U.S. When identifying a security risk, the FCC issues a denial of application, a power granted to it under Section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934. In China’s case, companies like China Telecom Corporation, China Unicom Operations Limited and Pacific Networks Corp. have all failed to secure FCC authorization for security reasons. "The Commission finds that due to several factors related to China Mobile USA’s ownership and control by the Chinese government, grant of the application would raise substantial and serious national security and law enforcement risks," the FCC wrote in its evaluation of China Mobile USA, a Delaware-based company. Even so, the FCC order does not address what the company needs to do with its hardware. "A Section 214 order is a license to sell regulated telecom service, not a physical eviction order," Harrigan’s office noted. Asked if he believes Republicans will be able to address the legislation before the end of the 119th Congress, Harrigan said he believes the issue will likely have to be left to the next session, which begins in January. FOREIGN ADVERSARIES RUNNING 'PSYOP' TO FUEL ANTI-AI AND ANTI-DATA CENTER MOVEMENT, WAR OFFICIAL SAYS He voiced optimism that the incoming Democratic majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate might recognize his bill as part of a larger interest in AI security. "This is a bipartisan problem. And there's a lot of work that I have done with my Democratic colleagues over this last year on artificial intelligence and the next generation of technology in our market economy and how that intertwines with our nation's defense," Harrigan said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They are very willing to lend a hand because they know it's a structural problem for our country," he added.

articles.title: "No lo tenían previsto": así han sido los 15 minutos más tensos entre el apretón de manos y el inicio del cara a cara entre Sánchez y Feijóo
articles.standfirst: 'La 1' ha confirmado que ese espacio de tiempo no se había contemplado como ocurrió
articles.summary: 'La 1' ha confirmado que ese espacio de tiempo no se había contemplado como ocurrió
articles.body: Los minutos previos al cara a cara entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo han estado marcados por la sorpresa en ambos bandos, "con esa tensión que ni siquiera se han saludado y finalmente sentados repasando apuntes". En la retransmisión de La 1, los periodistas desplazados recogieron las primeras impresiones de los equipos mientras los candidatos tomaban posiciones en el plató. Desde el entorno socialista admitieron que la duración del tramo previo les tomó por sorpresa: "Pues lo cierto es que no. Nos dicen que no sabían que esto iba a ser tan largo. Es lo que nos dicen ahora mismo desde el equipo de Pedro Sánchez. De momento, pues lo que estabais comentando, les está sorprendiendo tanto como a nosotros. Nos dicen literalmente que no sabían que iba a ser tan largo". A ello sumaron el mensaje de los barones regionales, convencidos de que el debate impulsará la movilización progresista y concentrará el apoyo en el PSOE, donde sostienen que "después de este cara a cara va a haber más gente que diga “yo sí te voy a votar, Pedro Sánchez". En el espacio de análisis, la presentadora Pepa recordó que esta contienda se libra en múltiples frentes antes de dar paso a la crónica desde el Partido Popular. Allí, Jara Laliena describió un ambiente igualmente expectante entre los populares ante las imágenes de su candidato en la tarima consultando papeles. Laliena explicó que el equipo de Feijóo buscaba aclarar lo ocurrido: "Pues, Pepa, acabamos de hacer precisamente esa consulta a Génova para que nos comenten si este escenario estaba sobre la mesa, si lo tenían previsto, pero por ahora no tenemos respuesta". Aunque admitió que "aquí hay nervios, nos reconocen algunas fuentes", subrayó que confían en el desarrollo del encuentro y en que se verá a "un presidente saliente" frente a "el presidente que necesita España". Finalmente, desde las filas populares pusieron el foco en los contenidos del debate y en el desgaste del rival. Según las fuentes consultadas, el PP logró imponer un bloque sobre corrupción pese a las reticencias socialistas, un punto en el que creen que el candidato del PSOE está preocupado, a la espera de confirmar si en Génova esperaban este escenario.

articles.title: Feijóo abre el debate arremetiendo contra Sánchez por los escándalos de la legislatura: "España merece un presidente decente y él no lo es"
articles.standfirst: El líder del PP abre el debate electoral con un duro ataque al presidente del Gobierno, al que reprocha los casos de corrupción, la falta de Presupuestos y la gestión de asuntos como la vivienda y los precios
articles.summary: El líder del PP abre el debate electoral con un duro ataque al presidente del Gobierno, al que reprocha los casos de corrupción, la falta de Presupuestos y la gestión de asuntos como la vivienda y los precios
articles.body: El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y el presidente del Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, se han enfrentado este jueves en el debate electoral a dos previo a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. El cara a cara, que se celebra en el plató de Tres Cantos de la Academia de la Televisión, está moderado por la presidenta de esta entidad, María Casado, y se prolongará durante aproximadamente dos horas. En ese tiempo, los candidatos a la Presidencia del Gobierno confrontarán sus propuestas en cinco bloques temáticos: Vivienda, Economía y Fiscalidad, Política Social y Servicios Públicos, Lucha contra la corrupción y Regeneración Democrática, y Migración y Política Exterior. Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha abierto el debate con un duro ataque a Pedro Sánchez durante su intervención sobre el balance de la legislatura. El líder del Partido Popular ha recurrido a las críticas de uno de los socios parlamentarios del presidente del Gobierno, Carles Puigdemont, para cuestionar su trayectoria política y poner en duda su credibilidad. Núñez Feijóo ha enumerado una larga lista de polémicas y asuntos controvertidos vinculados al Ejecutivo, entre ellos los casos Ábalos y Koldo, las informaciones sobre el hermano y la esposa de Sánchez, la gestión de la vivienda, la subida de los precios y la falta de Presupuestos Generales del Estado. También ha mencionado cuestiones relacionadas con el AVE, Adamuz, Toledo, Ceuta y El Hierro. "El balance lo ha hecho hoy uno de los socios de Sánchez. Puigdemont le define como persona amoral, cínica, con una ambición desmedida y capaz de vender España. La lista de escándalos es importante: Ábalos, Jéssica, orgías; Koldo, Leire, el hermano, la mujer, las cloacas, Zapatero, la vivienda, los precios, el infierno fiscal, si quieren recursos, que los pidan, ni un solo presupuesto, el AVE, Adamuz, Toledo, Ceuta y el Hierro", ha apuntado Núñez Feijóo. "Quieren que lo olvides, yo quiero que no vuelva a pasar. España merece un presidente decente y él no lo es", ha concluido el dirigente popular, que ha centrado su intervención en cuestionar la gestión del Gobierno y reclamar un cambio al frente del Ejecutivo.

images.caption: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, minutos antes del comienzo del debate con Pedro Sánchez. AP

articles.title: Trump’s pick for agency providing election security says Jan. 6 was not an attack
articles.summary: The nominee selected by President Donald Trump to lead the agency tasked with protecting elections in the U.S. refused Thursday to answer who won the 2020 presidential election or call the riot on Jan. 6, 2021, “an attack.”
articles.body: The nominee selected by President Donald Trump to lead the agency tasked with protecting elections in the U.S. refused Thursday to answer who won the 2020 presidential election or call the riot on Jan. 6, 2021, “an attack.” Michael LoSapio, who is nominated to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, was pressed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on the issues during a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee. Asked specifically who won the presidential race in 2020, LoSapio said, “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago.” “My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States,” he added, referencing Trump. Blumenthal accused LoSapio of “ducking the question in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity.” CISA has not had a director confirmed by the Senate since Trump returned to office in January 2025, when Jen Easterly vacated the role. The agency, which was established during the first Trump administration, was meant to protect the country’s critical infrastructure, including its elections, from hackers or cybercriminals. LoSapio, who serves as the chief information security officer at data and software company Palantir, was also asked whether there was an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6. Blumenthal pressed him on the issue, saying, “You don’t know?” “No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.” Blumenthal asked LoSapio about the nature of the riot once again, to which he maintained that “it was not an attack.” Trump’s own account of Jan. 6 has changed over the years, as he initially sought to distance himself from the riot, calling what happened “acts of violence and destruction” on Jan. 7, 2021. Though, as he hit the campaign trail in 2024, Trump shifted gears to call it a “day of love,” and later, when he returned to office, he pardoned roughly 1,500 people and commuted the sentences of another 14 in connection with the attack. Trump’s Justice Department also tried to launch a controversial “anti-weaponization” fund, which critics have called a “slush fund” to compensate the president’s allies. LoSapio is one of 13 nominees who appeared before the committee Thursday seeking to take over federal oversight, inspector general, Postal Service and District of Columbia Superior Court positions. To be confirmed as CISA director, LoSapio requires the committee to vote to advance his nomination to the full Senate, whose vote by a simple majority will determine whether he is confirmed. The clock is ticking for Trump nominees, as Democrats will take over control of Congress in January. The result of the 2020 presidential election has shaped CISA’s leadership. Trump fired its first director, Chris Krebs, just weeks after the election over his assertion that it was a secure race. LoSapio isn’t the first Trump nominee to skirt around questions regarding 2020’s presidential race. On Wednesday, Cody Hiland, Trump’s pick for a federal appeals court seat, told Blumenthal, “I’m not going to answer that,” when asked who won the election. Asked why he would not answer, Hiland said, “Because it’s going down a political track on an issue that happened six years ago, and I don’t want to come close to an ethical violation.” “We know the White House told you, ‘Don’t answer that question,’” Blumenthal responded.

images.caption: Michael LoSapio in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 19, 2026.

articles.title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders recalls ‘jarring’ encounter with angry mom who spat on her car
articles.summary: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders recalled a mom yelling in her face and spitting on her car at pre-K drop-off, a moment she says left her in shock.
articles.body: Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders recalled a "jarring" verbal assault she experienced at the hands of an angry mother while serving as White House press secretary during the first Trump administration. Sanders, who served as President Donald Trump’s White House press secretary from 2017 to 2019, relived an incident in which a mother berated her and spit on her car as she dropped off her toddler at school. "I was walking my youngest son into his pre-K class, and as I was going in, I'm holding his hand, another mom who has a child that's a 2- or 3-year-old in my son's class, kinda yells in my face, tells me what an awful human I am while standing next to my child and then turns and spits on our car," she said on a new episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity." MAHER CHALLENGES SARAH HUCKABEE SANDERS ON 'SOCIALISM' AS ARKANSAS GOVERNOR DEFENDS FREE SCHOOL BREAKFASTS The newly re-elected Arkansas governor said she had never been so "angry" and "disgusted," particularly because the woman scolded her in front of her toddler and other young children. "I was so, just, like, in shock. I'd never experienced something like that," she said. "It was so ... jarring and off-putting." Sanders, whose father, Mike Huckabee, serves as U.S. ambassador to Israel, said the encounter was among several difficult experiences she endured while working for Trump. She offered a glimpse into the price she paid working for the president during an especially politically contentious period. DANA PERINO SHARES HOW SHE SECRETLY PUSHED BACK AT REPORTERS DURING WHITE HOUSE BRIEFINGS During her final year in the administration, Sanders said she rarely ventured beyond the Trump International Hotel (now known as the Waldorf Astoria Washington DC) in Washington, D.C., which she described as a refuge from hostility she encountered elsewhere. She said she often feared restaurants would tamper with her food. "It was the only place that we could go and not get screamed at, or yelled at, or flipped off," Sanders said, saying the role of press secretary was the "hardest" job she ever had. "We could always get a table, and the food was good, and the people were nice and we knew they weren't spitting in our food," she added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Despite the hostility she encountered from critics of Trump, Sanders said she also experienced numerous positive interactions with people who commended her work in the administration. The governor said those interactions made the hard days "worth it." "Thankfully, for every one of those there were a hundred moments of people who would come up and say, ‘Thank you for standing with the president,’" Sanders said.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries wins overwhelming Speaker-designate vote as progressives' revolt falls flat
articles.summary: House Democrats unified behind Hakeem Jeffries with 251 of 262 secret ballots as 11 progressive holdouts demanded votes on ICE, Gaza and Citizens United.
articles.body: Democrats are fretting that the "Bloc" of progressives will lug House Democrats to the left. But, there is strength in numbers. Yours truly wanted to understand just how much sway progressives might have over the House Democratic Caucus. Look no further than Wednesday morning’s vote for speaker. No one challenged House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to become speaker-designate in the internal caucus vote. It’s about the math. Jeffries marshaled 251 of the 262 secret ballots cast. The recorded vote revealed that despite all of their noise and clamor, extreme progressives really don’t have much juice compared to the rest of the Democratic Caucus. In fact, rank-and-file Democrats crushed their progressive colleagues. Democrats did not vote by name. But numbers say a lot. While the recorded vote could have revealed potential craters of dissent among Democrats and questions about Jeffries, the tally registered the opposite. It showed just how diminutive the hard left is in the Democratic Caucus. JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER' Do they exude an outsized political voice? Yes. But success in Congress is measured in numbers. And at least on Wednesday, the numbers signaled few results for the Bloc and a show of unity among Democrats. "With the majority as big as it is, it's going to be very hard for anybody to try and hold our group of hostage," forecast Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.). "We’re going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people," said Jeffries. With more than 260 likely members in the Democratic Caucus, the Bloc wasn’t a factor on the first vote which mattered. In January, Jeffries becomes the 57th person and the first Black speaker to grip the gavel. Members of the Congressional Black Caucus celebrated the ascendency of their colleague. "I've been thinking about (the former Rep.) John Lewis (D-Ga.) a lot this week," said former House Majority Whip and Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), invoking the civil rights figure. "This is a very surreal moment for me." Clyburn spoke on behalf of Jeffries’ candidacy in the caucus, declaring that the path for the New York Democrat to the speakership makes him "feel vindicated." "As a Black woman from the South, having the next speaker of the House to be a Black man means a lot to me," said Rep. Nikema Williams (D-Ga.). Rep. Jonathan Jackson (D-Ill.) is the son of late Rev. Jesse Jackson. I asked what Jackson’s father would think of Jeffries rising to the speakership. "He’d be more than happy to see America making progress. This is what the world looks like. This is what America looks like," said Jackson. WATCH: JEFFRIES FACES UNCERTAINTY FROM INCOMING DEMOCRATS AS HOUSE SPEAKER VOTE APPROACHES But let’s filet the caucus vote for speaker to understand what unfolded with 11 Democrats who withheld their support from Jeffries. Representative-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) is a populist in a district which President Trump won by 10 points in 2024. Leonard defeated Rep. Mike Carey (R-Ohio). The district Leonard flipped in central Ohio is a long way politically from left-leaning districts in New York City and New Jersey where renegade members of the Bloc refused to cast their ballots for Jeffries. "What we need is a commitment from the speaker to get a 28th Amendment passed in 2028, to end Citizens United, end the corruption and call a vote on U.S. military aid to Israel," said Leonard. "If he does those things, he's got my vote." Seven of the progressives published a joint statement, demanding commitments from Jeffries to stop ICE and end "genocide in Gaza." The seven declared they saw "meaningful progress" in their talks with Jeffries. But since those negotiations continue, "our vote in caucus today was no" against Jeffries. Despite repeated efforts, none of the seven spoke to Fox. But what’s remarkable is that two of the seven withholding their support hail from Jeffries’ hometown, New York City. One is Representative-elect Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.) — who will represent a wide swath of Brooklyn and Queens. The other is Representative-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.). That district comprises parts of Upper Manhattan and The Bronx. Your trusty reporter tried to understand what the dissent meant. "How are their districts different than yours, being next door?" I asked Jeffries. He deflected. "The numbers speak for themselves," said Jeffries. I tried again. "But those districts — are they that different from what you represent? And yet they weren't willing to vote for you, Mr. speaker-designate?" No response. The lack of support for Jeffries from the dissidents annoyed Rep. Marilyn Strickland (D-Wash.). "This idea that Hakeem Jeffries has not earned this is completely absurd. He has worked hard. He's done everything he needed to do," said Strickland. Rep. Nydia Velázquez (D-N.Y.) is retiring at the end of this Congress. She opposed Valdez as her successor. She was bewildered that Valdez and Avila Chevalier wouldn’t support their hometown, Big Apple Congressman for speaker. "My advice to them is take the time to know how this institution runs and what it takes to be successful here," said an agitated Velázquez. Rep. Joe Morelle (D-N.Y.) served with Jeffries in the state legislature. He argued that Valdez and Avila Chevalier made a mistake. "They’re going to have to answer to their constituents," said Morelle. "I think they should have been with Hakeem Jeffries who’s led us to this historic majority." And if you aren’t on the team in politics, the team also isn’t on you. "It is a small group that marginalized themselves," said Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-Texas) about the holdouts. However, Representative-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) saw it differently. "They all got elected with very different constituencies. A lot of them have different priorities," said Koh. "There are things that their constituencies have demanded. And they want to make sure have the audience of the leader." Rep. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) believed there was strategy in the dissent. "They probably chose to do this because it's a way of lifting up their issues," said Landsman. And keep in mind, this wasn’t the actual vote for speaker. That comes on the floor in January. It’s a win-win for Jeffries and the holdouts if they forge an accord. He promises them certain votes. And they can then tout what they extracted from the next speaker. This is politics. But let’s put the 11 defections into context. Democrats flipped the House in 2018. In the internal caucus election, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) lost 32 votes. In the vote for speaker in January 2019, 12 Democrats voted for someone else. Three members voted present. "Nancy Pelosi will be remembered," said Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.). "And the 30 people who voted against her will not be remembered." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Jeffries will go down in the history books as the first Black speaker. The holdouts? They’re freshmen. As Moskowitz suggests, we’ll see if anyone recalls them in a few years.

articles.title: White House national cyber director is leaving the administration
articles.summary: Sean Cairncross has played a key role in crafting AI policy for the Trump administration. His immediate replacement is Kirsten A. Davies.
articles.body: White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving the Trump administration, a White House official confirmed Thursday. Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten A. Davies, who currently serves as the chief information officer at the Defense Department, a source close to the White House told NBC News. Davies will serve in an acting capacity, the source said. The position requires Senate confirmation. Axios was first to report the personnel changes. Cairncross has served as head of the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office oversees all government cybersecurity policy and strategy. He has been directly involved with the White House’s deliberations over AI policy, including after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directed Anthropic to take down its two most powerful AI systems over the summer due to national security concerns. Cairncross is leaving his post after a series of tech outages affected both private companies and government agencies over the past week. Administration officials as well as Democratic members of Congress have said the outages do not appear to be the result of cyberattacks, though some have suggested AI may have played a role. The White House, when reached for comment Thursday night, did not provide details about the staffing changes. Cairncross’ previous White House roles include senior adviser to the White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term. During the 2016 election cycle, Cairncross was the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer. He worked for the RNC again during the 2024 cycle, serving as then-chief operating officer Chris LaCivita’s deputy. The source close to the White House said Davies will strengthen the president’s cybersecurity team, which includes Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser. Rubio welcomed Davies to her new position in a social media post. “Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity,” Rubio wrote on X.

articles.title: Trump ousts cyber director after tech outages spark criticism
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White ‌House said on Thurs...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, a person close to the White ‌House said on Thursday, days after technology outages disrupted US air travel, banking ‌and national security systems.

The ouster comes as US President Donald Trump and his administration face ​mounting scrutiny over their response to the series of disruptions over the past week, including a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.

The dismissal of Cairncross dismissal ‌is the administration's first major ⁠personnel move since the outages.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer ⁠Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.

"The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition ​of anonymity.

Cairncross ​said in a statement on Thursday night it ​was the "honor of a lifetime ‌to serve" in Trump's administration.

The recent technology disruptions are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, cybersecurity experts told Reuters. Advanced AI tools make it easier for companies to uncover weaknesses in their cybersecurity protections.

The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions were ‌separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical ​changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored ​attack.

Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri ​on Tuesday told reporters in Washington the Trump administration should ‌brief lawmakers on the outages so ​they can "share with ​the American people what's happening here."

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need ​to be confirmed by ‌the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in ​January.

(Reporting by Courtney Rozen and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by ​Caitlin Webber, John Mair and Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title: Senate passes sweeping bill simplifying permitting rules to build in America
articles.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects. The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, was crafted by an unusual coalition of Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. The legislation would revise and speed up environmental reviews with tighter deadlines; accelerate electricity transmission; restrict the power of federal agencies to revoke existing permits; and reduce chokepoints for approving and completing projects. To conservatives, it’s about cutting government bureaucracy. “For far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty,” Capito said. For liberals, it’s an opportunity to make it easier to build long-sought projects, including clean energy, and address high costs. “Democrats are focused on lowering energy costs, reducing emissions, and stopping data centers’ free ride,” Whitehouse said. “Americans will start to get some relief quickly if this bill passes.” In an attempt to alleviate Americans’ concerns about data centers, the bill would require “new data centers of 20 megawatts or more to pay the full incremental cost of the infrastructure built to serve them,” according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. The legislation sparked opposition from some environmental groups and Native American tribal organizations, which objected to easing reviews and consultation rules that can be used to protect their interests. The bulk of the opposition in the Senate came from Democrats. Still, the willingness to simplify permitting rules represents a philosophical shift for the Democrats who endorsed it. Part of the reason is that liberal policy experts recognized that existing laws hinder their own goals. “This removes a lot of the obstacles that hamstrung [Joe] Biden’s climate investments,” said Adam Jentleson, a former Senate Democratic aide and founder of the research group Searchlight Institute. “A big part of the Inflation Reduction Act — a lot of the projects couldn’t break ground because of all the red tape.” The bill still needs approval from the House, where Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., expressed optimism that Congress will send a bill to President Donald Trump’s desk. “Well, we want to see a bill pass both chambers,” Scalise said when asked if the House will take up the Senate version of the legislation. “Obviously, the details matter. ... Hopefully, they pass a good bill back, and if not, we’ll work out those differences. But we want to get a bill to the president’s desk, and that’s still got a great chance to happen.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the clearest path to making a law is for the House to take the Senate’s measure and pass it, noting that it has been through extensive debate. “It has been litigated now for months. Continues to be,” Thune told reporters. “Everything gets more complicated over here procedurally, and if it were to go over there and then come back over here, I can’t predict what happens. So hopefully there’ll be the critical mass there to move it. ... It’s been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process.”

images.caption: From left, Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., hold a news conference on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.
